                                           CHAPTER 7

                              AIRCRAFT SORTIE STATISTICS


7-1. INTRODUCTION. This chapter presents statistics on Soviet and German aircraft sortie
activity during the KDB campaign. The KDB records a daily listing of the number of sorties
generated for each aircraft type/mission type combination. Neither numbers of onhand aircraft,
armament delivered, nor specific targets attacked are comprehensively recorded in the KDB.
Therefore, only total daily air sorties are summarized here according to armed combat roles
(attack, bombing, or air-to-air) as well as unarmed roles (reconnaissance, evacuation). Each
aircraft sortie was assigned only one role. The attack role applies to air attack against specific
tactical targets, much like contemporary close air support. The bombing role applies to attacks
against less specific area targets, similar to contemporary interdiction. Except for eight Soviet
sorties in missions categorized as "special" in the KDB, all aircraft sorties recorded in the KDB
are summarized in this chapter.

assigned to each role, and Table 7-2 shows the types of Soviet aircraft assigned to each role. No
Soviet evacuation sorties are recorded in the KDB.

7-3. SORTIE ACTIVITY

    a. Total Sorties. Figure 7-1 shows total sorties generated in each role during the KDB
campaign. The column labeled "ALL" is the sum of plotted sortie totals in the five roles and
includes all KDB sorties except for eight Soviet sorties categorized as "special." Summary
observations include:

       (1) The Germans generated slightly more total sorties than the Soviets.

       (2) The roles with the most sorties were ground attack for the Germans and air-to-air for
the Soviets, which accounted for 48 percent of each combatant's total sorties. The Germans
generated over twice as many ground attack sorties as the Soviets, but the Soviets had twice as
many air-to-air sorties as the Germans.

       (3) Both combatants had about 4,000 bombing sorties (3,800 German, 4,500 Soviet).

       (4) There were 1,400 German evacuation sorties, but none for the Soviets.

                                           CHAPTER 8

                    GEOGRAPHIC UNIT POSITIONS AND PROGRESS


8-1. INTRODUCTION. This chapter presents charts of average German progress during the
campaign, along with charts containing digitized geographic overlays of individual unit
positions, with personnel and tank attrition results for individual units attached to the overlays in
a geographically correlated format. Unit positions were calculated from data in the unit location
file of the KDB. Daily unit positions recorded for German and Soviet units in the KDB are listed
in Appendix L. Unit locations in the KDB are represented as a set of (up to 18) reference point
locations associated with that unit. The unit position was computed as the arithmetic average of
all ofthat unit's reference point locations in the KDB, excluding the unit HQ (which usually lay
to the rear of the other unit points).

8-2. AVERAGE GERMAN FORCE PROGRESS. Figure 8-1 shows the daily cumulative
(since 4 July) average and maximum northbound progress, in km, of the German line units in
contact with the enemy. Figure 8-2 shows the daily change (from the previous day) in both
average and maximum northbound progress.

    a. Methodology. On each day, the cumulative average northbound progress is calculated as
the arithmetic average, over the German line units, of the change in latitude (expressed in km),
since 4 July, of each unit location. The cumulative maximum northbound progress on a day is
computed, in km, as the largest change in latitude, since 4 July, over the German line unit
positions on that day. It is the largest northbound movement, since 4 July, made by a single
German unit, as opposed to the average movement over the line units. On the chart, the short
unit ID of the German unit with largest northbound movement (since 4 July) on a day is printed
above the bar graph for that day.

   b. Summary Results

        (1) Cumulative Progress. Both average and maximum progress peaked on 16 July
when 7 Pz Division had advanced 46 km north of its initial position, while overall average
progress along the German front was 21 km. Cumulative average German progress increased
steadily until 16 July and then leveled off through 18 July. Maximum progress declined from 46
km to 41 km on 18 July when 7 Pz Division shifted position.

        (2) Daily Change in Progress. Figure 8-2 shows the daily change (from the previous
day) in both average and maximum German northbound advance. Northbound advance is a
suitable measure of progress because the primary German objective was a northward advance
toward Kursk. Average German northbound progress increased every day, except for 17 July,
but daily changes after 13 July were less than 1 km. The largest single day gain in average
progress was 3.3 km on 8 July. The largest changes in maximum northbound progress were
gains of 9 km on 7 July and 8 km on 10 July. These two days accounted for almost 40 percent of
the maximum German northbound progress over the entire KDB campaign.

8-3. PROGRESS OF GERMAN FORWARD POSITIONS. In this report, the locations of
the single northernmost German reference point in the line units on a specified day are treated
and denoted as the forward edge of the battle area (FEBA) of the German force on that day.
Lines connecting the points comprising this German FEBA for 4,8,12, and 18 July are shown
on a digitized map (circa 1993) of the Kursk area in Figure 8-3, which was constructed using the
US Army's Terrain Evaluation Module. The figure shows that most of the advance during the
campaign had been achieved by 8 July. The German movements toward the northwest on 9-12
July and toward the northeast on 12-18 July are apparent in the map.

8-4. GEOGRAPHIC REPRESENTATION OF UNIT POSITIONS AND ATTRITION.
Figure 3-5 showed a TEM-generated digitized map plot of German and Soviet line unit positions
on 4 July. Arrows drawn on that map indicate the path of the primary German advance. Figures
8-4 through 8-7 were created using a combination of TEM and Microsoft Excel. As in Figure
3-5, Soviet unit symbols are drawn with a double line box boundary, while German unit symbols
have only a single line box boundary. The abbreviated unit name is printed to the lower left of
the associated unit symbol. The abbreviated unit name is from the short unit IDs listed in Tables
3-1 and 3-2. The figures show unit positions, along with unit personnel casualty rates and unit
tank losses, on 5 July, 8 July, 12 July, and 18 July. These figures are denoted herein as
"geographs." Geographs enable a spatial as well as quantitative view of losses over units on a
day. Along with unit positions on the specified day, each geograph also shows a line through the
unit positions on the previous day. Arrows are also drawn along the German advance. In these
geographs, a small scatter plot is drawn above each map which shows, for each plotted circle
(Soviet) or square (German), the casualty rate (combat casualties/1,000 men) on that day for a
unit on the map which lies on a vertical line through the plotted circle/square. Analogously, a
scatter plot is drawn below each map, showing, for each plotted circle (Soviet), or square
(German), the number of tanks destroyed (including abandoned) on that day for a unit on the
map lying on a vertical line through the plotted circle/square. For example, the left plotted circle


                                                                                                 8-3
CAA-SR-98-7

in each scatter plot in Figure 8-4 plots losses in the Soviet 237 RD, the leftmost Soviet unit on
the map, while the leftmost black square plots losses for German 57 ID, the leftmost German unit
on the map. Bar graphs to the right of the map show total combat casualties and tanks lost
(destroyed + abandoned) for the total force, as well as the average combat casualty rate over all
engaged line units which had combat casualties that day. Battle summary narratives describing,
in present tense, combat events and statistics associated with each geograph are given below.
Unit postures noted in these narratives are those recorded in the KDB on that day.

      a. 5 July Geograph (Figure 8-4)

        (1) Combat Postures/Dispositions. German 168 ID, 255 ID, and 57 ID are in prepared
defenses. The 198th ID has not yet entered the theater. All other German line units are
attacking. Only one Soviet unit (213 RD) is attacking.

        (2) Progress. Only German 48 Pz Corps makes significant progress, but it incurs 16 of
the 23 total German tank losses while destroying 28 tanks in 67 Gds RD. The most forward
German unit, which also makes the greatest northernmost progress (8 km), is 167 ID in 48 Pz
Corps.

        (3) Tank Losses. Total Soviet tanks lost (86) are almost 4 times German losses (23).
The 2 SS Pz Corps destroys 25 tanks in 52 Gds RD while losing only 2 tanks. Most Soviet tank
losses (53) are M-3 tanks in 57 Gds RD and 67 Gds RD. The 167 Tank Rgt, attached to 25 Gds
Rifle Corps, loses 26 T-34s. The 14 destroyed Pz V tanks in Gross Deutschland PzGrD (GDPZ)
account for the majority of German losses. Recorded as damaged in action today are 179
German tanks and only 19 Soviet tanks.

        (4) Personnel Losses. Total German and Soviet casualties are similar, but since 62
percent of the full Soviet force is not in contact with the enemy, Soviet casualty rates in engaged
units are much higher than German. German 48 Pz Corps inflicts massive casualties on 71 Gds
RD and 67 Gds RD, which lose over 10 percent of personnel. The Soviet unit with worst
casualties is 78 Gds RD, on the Soviet left, which loses almost 20 percent of its personnel.
Highest German casualty rates are on the right flank in 106 ID and 320 ID, which lose 6 percent
and 8 percent of personnel, respectively.

      b. 8 July Geograph (Figure 8-5)

        (1) Combat Postures/Dispositions. The far German left is unchanged, with 255 ID
assuming a hasty defense posture today after 2 days attacking. German 57 ID, 167 ID, and 320
ID are in prepared defenses. Localized Soviet counterattacks force Das Reich SS PzGrD
(DRSS), Totenkopf SS PzGrD (TSS), and 7 PzD to shift into hasty defense today. Nine German
line units are attacking. The German 198th ID is not on line yet. Much Soviet armor (31 Tank
Corps, 192 Tank Bde, 86 Tank Bde, 10 Tank Corps, 2 Gds Tank Corps, 5 Gds Tank Corps) has
moved up to stop the advance of 2 SS Pz Corps. Soviet 6 Tank Corps has moved up to stop 48th
Pz Corps. Soviet 5 Gds Tank Corps, 2 Gds Tank Corps, and 15 Gds RD have begun
counterattacking. All other Soviet line units are in defensive postures.

        (2) Progress. German 48 Pz Corps and 2 SS Pz Corps have made significant advances,
with northbound progress of 5.3 km (11 PzD) and 7.8 km (Leibstandarte SS, also denoted as
LSSAH) during the day. In 3 Pz Corps, both 6 PzD and 7 PzD have advanced 6-7 km north
during the day. Largest northward progress since 4 July was made by Das Reich (22 km) and
Leibstandarte SS (23 km), which is the most forward unit of the force. Average northward
progress of the entire German force is 3 km for the day and 10 km since 4 July.

        (3) Tank Losses. Four Soviet units (3 MC, 31 TC, 6 TC, and 5 Gds TC) account for 194
of the total Soviet tank losses (215), which is much greater than the German loss total (16). Most
of the German losses are Pz III (seven) and Pz IV (five). Most of the Soviet losses (159) are T-
34 tanks. Heaviest German tank losses are in Das Reich, which loses six tanks. Highest Soviet
tank losses (64) are in 3 Mech Corps (3MC). Recorded as damaged in action today are 93
German tanks and 100 Soviet tanks.

        (4) Personnel Losses. Total Soviet combat casualties (9,400) are over 3 times German
(2,800). Highest German casualty rates are on the right flank in 19 Pz D and 7 Pz D, which lose
2 percent of personnel. Highest Soviet casualty rates are in 52 Gds RD and 67 Gds RD, which
lose over 10 percent of personnel

   c. 12 July Geograph (Figure 8-6)

        (1) Combat Postures/Dispositions. Many Soviet line units (25 of 48) are counter-
attacking today, most of them concentrated to stop the 48 Pz Corps and 2 SS Pz Corps in the
center. All other online Soviet units are in defense postures, most (15) in hasty defense. Most of
the counterattacking Soviet units (21 of 25) are forced into hasty defense postures by 14 July.
German 198 ID came on line on 10 July. The German 167 ID, 255 ID, 320 ID, and 57 ID are in
prepared defenses. Das Reich and Grossdeutschland (GDPZ) are forced in hasty defense. All
other German line units are attacking.

        (2) Progress. German 48 Pz Corps and 2 SS Pz Corps have made progress since 8 July,
but their advance has stalled, with 1 lPzD and Totenkopf SS in the lead. Recent progress has
been made on the German right by 6 Pz D, which has moved 11.4 km farther north in 1 day but
is surrounded by Soviet units. Although average northward progress for the day for the entire
German force is 2 km, four German units (57 ID, 3 PzD, 198 ID, GDPZ) moved an average 2 km
south today. The largest northward advances since July 8 were made by Totenkopf SS (30 km)
and 6 PzD (22 km). Average German northward progress since 4 July is 16.5 km. Largest
northward progress since 4 July was made by Totenkopf SS (40 km) and 11 PzD (32 km), which
is the most forward unit of the force. The German line will advance no farther north after today,
with 11 PzD and Totenkopf SS holding the northernmost positions through 18 July.

       (3) Tank Losses. Total Soviet tank losses (204) are over 20 times German (9). The vast
majority of today's tank conflicts are near Prokhorovka, where the counterattacking Soviet 29
Tank Corps, 18 Tank Corps, and 2 Gds Tank Corps lose a total of 144 tanks against




                                                                                               8-5
CAA-SR-98-7

Leibstandarte SS, Totenkopf SS, and Das Reich, which lose a total of 6 tanks (4 Pz III and 5 Pz
IV). Highest Soviet tank losses (88) are in 29 Tank Corps, which loses 60 T-34s and 28 T-70s.
Highest German tank losses (four) are in Leibstandarte SS. Most of the Soviet losses are T-34s
(119), T-70 (61), and MK-4 Churchill (13). Recorded as damaged in action today are 89 German
tanks and 210 Soviet tanks.

        (4) Personnel Losses. Total Soviet combat casualties (19,400) are almost 8 times the
German total (2,450). Soviet casualties are very high on their left flank, with 270 RD and 73
Gds RD losing over 15 percent of personnel. The Soviet unit with the worst losses (28 percent)
is 184 RD. Highest German casualty rates are in the center, with 167 ID losing 3 percent of
personnel and Leibstandarte SS losing 2 percent.

      d. 18 July Geograph (Figure 8-7)

        (1) Combat Postures/Dispositions. All German units have been in defensive postures
since 17 July. The last German unit to cease attacks was 7 PzD, which moved northwest into
defensive posture on 17 July under 48 Pz Army. Combat intensity has fallen sharply since 12
July. The Soviet counteroffensive resumes today, with 11 line units attacking (up from only 2
attackers on 17 July).

        (2) Progress. German 48 Pz Corps and 2 SS Pz Corps have been stalled since 12 July,
with 11 PzD and Totenkopf SS continually holding the northernmost positions. 3 Pz Corps has
made progress, with 19 PzD advancing 19 km north on the right flank since 12 July. Although
the northernmost German unit is 11 PzD, the German unit with greatest northward progress (41
km) since 4 July is 7 PzD. Only three German units (11 PzD, DRSS, and LSSAH) are farther
south (by less than 3 km) on 18 July than on 12 July. Average northward progress of the entire
German force is 0.3 km for the day and 21 km since 4 July.

        (3) Tank Losses. Total Soviet tank losses of 27 are light, but no German losses are
reported. Almost all Soviet losses are T-34 (18) and T-70 (8). Soviet tank losses are
concentrated in 18 Tank Corps, 29 Tank Corps, 2 Tank Corps, and 2 Gds Tank Corps, all of
which attack, losing a total of 24 tanks. No German losses are reported. Recorded as damaged
in action today are 6 German tanks and 58 Soviet tanks.

        (4) Personnel Losses. Total Soviet combat casualties (3,200) are 3 times the German
losses (900). Soviet casualties are relatively light, with the highest casualty rate (5 percent of
personnel) in 2 Gds Tank Corps. German casualties are also very light, with 167 ID having the
highest rate (1 percent of personnel).

                                          CHAPTER 9

                                       OBSERVATIONS


9-1. PURPOSE. The purpose of this chapter is to address the essential elements of analysis
specified in the study directive by summarizing the observations noted in the previous chapters.
The overall objective is to construct a campaign summary of the southern front of the Kursk
Battle from the assessed statistical results and trends derived from the KDB.

9-2. ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF ANALYSIS. In response to the following study EEA,
summary observations were developed from the results and analysis in Chapters 3 through 8:

   a. What are results and trends from the KDB for units and combat posture status?

        (1) Force Composition. The German force in the southern front Kursk Battle consisted
of seven German headquarters units, eight infantry divisions, five Panzer divisions, and four
Panzer Grenadier divisions. The Soviet force consisted of 19 Soviet headquarters units, 35 rifle
divisions, 8 tank corps, 2 mechanized corps, 2 airborne divisions, and 1 detachment.

        (2) German Combat Postures. The majority of the German units were continually
attacking from 5 July through 12 July, but all ceased attacking by 17 July, when almost all were
in prepared defenses. The recorded maximum German offensive efforts were on 6 July and 11
July.

        (3) Soviet Combat Postures. The maximum Soviet counteroffensive efforts were on 12
July and 18 July. The vast majority of Soviet line units were in defensive postures on all days
except 12 July, when they counterattacked. After the 12 July counterattack, the vast majority of
attacking Soviet units shifted into hasty defense postures by 14 July.

        (4) Fraction in Active Combat. A considerably larger fraction of the German line units
was engaged in combat and incurring casualties for a longer time than was the case for Soviet
line units. More than half of Soviet line units were not in active combat from 4-10 July and 15-
18 July.

   b. What are results and trends from the KDB for army personnel status and
casualties?

      (1) Fraction Personnel Engaged. Over 5-18 July, an average of 92 percent of the
German manpower was engaged, versus an average 67 percent for the Soviets.

      (2) Permanent versus Temporary Casualties. The effect of a large German advantage
in number of KIA is offset by near parity in "temporary" loss rates (fraction of force wounded).

      (3) Differences in Casualties. From 5-18 July, Soviet casualties were much greater than
German. Relative to initial onhand, total casualties amounted to 23 percent of the Soviet force



                                                                                              9-1
CAA-SR-98-7

Overall, the Soviets lost (KIA) nearly 5 men killed for every German killed and 24 CMIA for
every German CMIA.

       (4) Daily Casualty Rates. If daily average combat casualty rates are averaged over the 5
July-18 July period, the overall Soviet rate was 4 times the German rate.

        (5) Exposure to Combat Fatigue. After 4 July, all German line units in the theater
were taking casualties, but, on average, almost 30 percent of Soviet line units were not taking
casualties during this period. Over 5-18 July, an average of 92 percent of the German manpower
was in contact with enemy forces, versus an average 67 percent for the Soviets.

         (6) Fractional Exchange Ratios. Soviet/German FER results computed in favor of
Germans, based on both KCMIA casualties and on combat casualties, show that the Germans
almost always had an advantage (FER >1). The KCMIA FER exceeds 4.00 on 9 days.
However, the historical battle outcome suggests that this was not enough to achieve a decisive
victory.

      c. What are results and trends from the KDB for army weapons status and losses?

       (1) Initial Force Level Comparison. At the start of the campaign, the Germans were
outnumbered at least 2:1 in tanks and at least 3:1 in heavy AT weapons and light infantry support
weapons (machineguns, mortars, and light AT). Initial German parity or superiority in initial
inventory existed only for artillery, rockets, APC, and antiaircraft weapon classes.

         (2) Beginning Assets versus Ending Assets

             (a) Ending (18 July) German onhand tank assets were about 50 percent of initial
onhand levels, but all other German weapon classes had ending onhand assets close to their
initial (4 July) levels.

             (b) Ending Soviet tank levels were 40 percent of initial levels, and ending AT
weapon and infantry support weapon (mortar, flame/MG) asset levels were about one-third lower
than initial. The heavy losses in Soviet minor weapons were probably due to entire units being
overrun during the German advance.

             (c) Soviet artillery, antiaircraft, and rocket launcher onhand assets on 18 July were
close to initial levels.

        (3) Weapons in Contact. From 5-18 July, an average 98 percent of onhand German
tanks and 97 percent of German heavy AT weapons were in contact with the enemy, as opposed
to an average of only 64 percent of Soviet tanks, and only 67 percent of Soviet heavy AT.

        (4) Soviet: German Loss Ratios. German AA losses and rocket launcher losses were
greater than Soviet losses, but the Soviets lost far more in all other categories. Overall, the
Germans killed (destroyed) six Soviet tanks for every tank they lost. SovietGerman loss ratios




9-2
                                                                                     CAA-SR-98-7


(for destroyed weapons) over the entire campaign were very high for heavy AT (8:1), light AT
(70:1), mortars (16:1), and flame/MG (20:1).

        (5) Ratios of Damaged to Destroyed Weapons

         (a) The ratio of damaged to destroyed weapons exceeded 1.00 for five of the nine
German weapon classes, but for only one Soviet weapon class.

         (b) There were 5.6 damaged German tanks for every destroyed German tank and 2.5
damaged German heavy AT weapons for every destroyed German AT weapon.

          (c) The Soviet ratios of damaged to destroyed tanks and damaged to destroyed heavy
AT were less than 1.00.

        (6) Fractional Exchange Ratios. The Soviet/German FERs for tanks and for heavy AT
weapons, computed in favor of the Germans and based on destroyed weapons, are much greater
than the comparable FERs based on [destroyed + damaged] weapons.

    d. What are results and trends from the KDB for ammunition status?

        (1) Onhand Inventory. Artillery and small arms/AA accounted for the majority (71
percent) of initial German inventory tonnage, while artillery and tank/AT ammo comprised most
(64 percent) of the initial Soviet tonnage. German daily onhand tank/AT, artillery, rocket, and
small arms AA ammunition inventory levels were always higher that Soviet.

         (2) Consumption. Over the total KDB campaign, the Soviets consumed 44 percent
more tank/AT ammunition than the Germans. The Germans expended three times the Soviet
artillery tonnage, two times the Soviet rocket tonnage, and three times the Soviet small arms/AA
tonnage expenditure. Artillery accounted for the largest portion of both forces' ammunition
tonnage consumed.

   e. What are results and trends from the KDB for aircraft sortie status?

       (1) Aircraft Roles. The Germans generated more total sorties than the Soviets. The
roles with the most sorties were ground attack for the Germans and air-to-air for the Soviets,
which accounted for almost half of each combatant's total sorties.

        (2) Air-ground Activity. On most days, German air-to-ground activity exceeded Soviet
activity. Most German air-to-ground sorties were in the ground attack role, while the majority of
Soviet air-to-ground sorties were in the (area) bombing role.

       (3) Air-to-air Activity. Soviet air-to-air activity always exceeded German activity. The
day-to-day variation in Soviet air-to-air activity was extremely similar to the day-to-day variation
in German air-to-ground activity.




                                                                                                 9-3
CAA-SR-98-7

       (4) Reconnaissance Activity. German air reconnaissance activity was usually higher
than Soviet.

   f. What are results and trends from the KDB for geographic unit positions and
German progress?

         (1) Cumulative Progress

           (a) Both average and maximum German progress peaked on 16 July when elements
of 7 Pz Division had advanced 46 km north of their 4 July position, while overall average
progress was 21 km.

            (b) Cumulative average German progress increased steadily until 16 July, and then
leveled off through 18 July.

         (2) Daily Change in Progress

            (a) Average (over units) German northbound progress increased every day, except
for 17 July, but daily changes after 13 July were less than 1 km. The largest single day gain in
average German northbound progress was 3.3 km on 8 July.

           (b) The largest daily changes in German maximum (over units) northbound progress
were gains of 9 km on 7 July and 8 km on 10 July. These 2 days accounted for almost 40 percent
of the maximum German northbound progress over the entire KDB campaign.

      g. What aspects of combat appeared to significantly affect historical battle outcome?

        (1) Relationship Between Permanent and Temporary Personnel Losses. The effect
of a large German advantage in number of "permanent" (KIA) kills was offset by near parity in
"temporary" loss rates (fraction of force wounded). Since the initial Soviet force was almost
double the size of the Germans, a campaign of attrition could not produce a decisive German
victory with these casualty rates.

        (2) Personnel Fatigue from Close Combat. The Germans had a considerably larger
portion of their force in contact and taking casualties than did the Soviets. This suggests that the
German force was subjected to more fatigue from the effects of nearly constant combat than was
its opponent. Also, since rest and replenishment were minimal in such a heavily committed
force, the effectiveness and efficiency of German combat elements probably deteriorated over
time relative to the Soviet force.

       (3) Lack of Mechanized Reserves. With an average of 97+ percent of its heavy
mechanized force on the front lines, the Germans, unlike the Soviets, had no reserves on which
to draw. The combat quality of the German mechanized weapon systems probably deteriorated
from continual combat without rest and replenishment.




9-4
                                                                                  CAA-SR-98-7


       (4) Relationship Between Permanent and Temporary Tank Losses. The
Soviet:German ratio of [destroyed tanks + damaged tanks not returned] is only 2.66, which is
considerably less than the 6:1 Soviet:German ratio of tanks destroyed. Although favorable to the
Germans, it was not enough to achieve a decisive victory.

       (5) Insufficiently Favorable Fractional Exchange Ratios. A very high FER was
required to achieve annihilation, but high FERs were sporadic and not sustained. In addition, the
Soviets always had unengaged reserves, while the Germans were always fully committed and
engaged.

                                                          CAA-SR-98-7

                                      APPENDIX B

                                 STUDY DIRECTIVE


MEMORANDUM FOR: DIRECTOR, US ARMY CONCEPTS ANALYSIS AGENCY
                 8120 WOODMONT AVENUE, BETHESDA, MD 20814

SUBJECT: Kursk Operation Simulation and Validation Exercise (KOSAVE) Study - Phase II


1. PURPOSE OF DIRECTIVE. This Directive provides for the conduct of a study to develop
and document a statistical record of the World War II (WWII) Battle of Kursk, based on the
Kursk Data Base (KDB) containing historical data describing the battle.

2. STUDY TITLE: Kursk Operation Simulation and Validation Exercise (KOSAVE) Study -
Phase II (KOSAVE II)

3. BACKGROUND.

     a. In 1995, CAA completed the Ardennes Campaign Simulation (ARCAS) Study. ARC AS
compared a simulation of the 1944-45 Ardennes Campaign of World War II (WW II). with
historical data from the Ardennes Campaign Simulation Data Base (ACSDB) a computerized
data base campaign derived from archival historical records. ARCAS was a novel use of a
comprehensive data base of historical data from a large-scale real world campaign which set
initial conditions for a model validation exercise using a fully automated campaign model. The
stochastic combat simulation tested in the ARCAS analysis was the Stochastic CEM (STOCEM)
model, a stochastic version of the Concepts Evaluation Model VII (CEM VII). Valuable
information and observations on simulation model behavior and guidelines for CAA model
changes and improvements have resulted from the ARCAS effort.

    b. The ARCAS results are only a first step in the Model-Test-Model paradigm of validation
methodology which uses model test and evaluation results in an iterative process of successive
model improvement with each successive step increasing overall validity. A different historical
campaign is a necessary baseline for an operational (re-)test of an improved STOCEM, and will
also provide additional insights on simulation behavior and credibility. In light of this
requirement, Director, CAA, proposed that, concurrent with the ARCAS, a history data base of
another WW II battle should be constructed as a precursor to execution of a follow-on validation
effort, with objectives analogous to those of ARCAS, which could be used to test and refine the
results from ARCAS.

    c. In 1993, The Dupuy Institute was issued a contract to construct a comprehensive history
data base of the Southern Front of the WW II Battle of Kursk. This data base, designated as the
Kursk Data Base (KDB), was completed in September, 1996. The WW II Battle of Kursk is
designated as the historical campaign for use in testing and assessing the predictive value of
STOCEM. The Southern Kursk Battle will be simulated with the STOCEM, using the KDB as
input. Simulation results will then be compared with history data, and subsequently used to test,
verify, modify, and extend observations and model modification guidelines developed from
ARCAS.




                                                                                                    B-l
CAA-MR-97-51




          d. Prior to setting up and executing the combat simulation, an historical baseline must be
      created from the KDB. The KOSAVE Study (Phase II) is will generate a statistical record of the
      Kursk Battle from the KDB which can serve as both a baseline for the simulation scenario, and
      as a standalone historical record.

      4. STUDY SPONSOR AND STUDY DIRECTOR. KOSAVE is a CAA in-house study. The
      study sponsor is the Director, U.S. Army Concepts Analysis Agency. The study director is Mr.
      Walter J. Bauman.

      5. PERFORMING AGENCY. U.S. Army Concepts Analysis Agency (USACAA).

      6. PURPOSE. The purpose of the KOSAVE Study (Phase II) is to develop and document a
      statistical record of the Kursk Battle from the KDB for use as both a baseline for simulation
      comparison, and as a standalone descriptive record for historians

      7. OBJECTIVES. Assess results and trends from the KDB for the following aspects of the
      Kursk Battle:

         a. units and combat posture status

         b. personnel status and casualties.

         c. army weapons status and losses,

         d ammunition status.

         e. aircraft sortie status.

         f. geographic unit positions and progress.

      8. SCOPE.

       a. The base campaign scenario used in the combat simulation is the Southern Front of the
      WWII Battle of Kursk, as represented in the KDB historical data.

          b. Only results and data for combat units in the KDB will be included. Noncombat support
      units will not be covered.

      9. TIMEFRAME. The scenario timeframe is from 4 July 1943 (denoted as D-Day) through 18
      July 1943.

      10. LIMITATIONS.

         a. Results will not be expressed in terms of specific KDB weapon types. Weapons will be
      aggregated into categories or classes for tractability.




B-2
                                                                                               CAA-SR-98-7




    b. The accuracy of results directly reflects, and depends on, the accuracy of the KDB
collection process. Any errors in the KDB will be carried over into quantification summaries and
results.

    c. Human factors (e.g. fatigue, caution, aggressiveness) regulating the pace and intensity of
battle were not quantifiable.

11. ASSUMPTIONS.

   a. The Kursk Data Base accurately represents the status and structure of forces in the
Southern Front of the actual WWII Battle of Kursk

   b. The personnel casualty and system kill criteria used to categorize KDB casualty and
weapon loss are sufficiently consistent to allow meaningful reporting and comparisons between
combatants.

   c. The use of interpolation techniques between irregular reports in historical records to
enable and create a complete set of daily report records in the KDB is reasonable.

12. ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF ANALYSIS (EEA).

    a. What are results and trends from the KDB for units and combat posture status?

    b. What are results and trends from the KDB for personnel status and casualties?

    c. What are results and trends from the KDB for army weapons status and losses?

    d. What are results and trends from the KDB for ammunition status?

    e. What are results and trends from the KDB for aircraft sorties?

   f. What are results and trends from the KDB for geographic unit positions and German
progress?

    g. What aspects of combat appeared to significantly affect historical battle outcome?

13. RESPONSIBILITIES. Since this is an internal study, CAA will direct the study, obtain the
necessary data, perform required analyses, organize results, and document the study.

                                          APPENDIX D

                      COMBAT UNIT ATTACHMENTS IN THE KDB


D-l. INTRODUCTION. The tables in this appendix show the unit ID of all German and
Soviet combat units in the KDB and indicate which KDB units below division level were
attached to higher level primary combat units, and which were unattached nondivisional units
operating independently. Most units recorded in the KDB on a day were recorded therein as
attached to one of the primary combat units listed in Tables 3-1 and 3-2, Chapter 3. Two dummy
unit names have been created to refer to the collective total, in each force, of combat units which
are not attached to any other unit. The dummy unit named UNATTACHED is listed as a parent
to all units which, according to the KDB, were not attached to any parent unit on a given day, but
which were attached to a parent unit on at least one other day of the campaign. The dummy unit
named OTHER NONDIV is listed as a parent to all units which, according to the KDB, are never
attached to any parent unit at any time during the entire KDB campaign.

D-2. ATTACHMENT RELATIONSHIPS. Tables D-l and D-2 are not in conflict with
Tables 3-4 and 3-5, which show each combatant's order or battle. Tables D-l and D-2 show
attachment relationships of units below division level which are primarily associations formed to
achieve combined and coordinated operations and support at a maneuver level. These
relationships differ from those in Tables 3-4 and 3-5, which show hierarchical order of battle
subordination of units at the strategic planning level. They do not show recorded attachments of
units at division and corps level to higher units because they are intended to show only positional
groupings of units operating together as part of a primary combat unit.

D-3. GERMAN COMBAT UNIT ATTACHMENTS. Table D-l shows attachment rules for
all 75 German combat units in the KDB. Each unit is numbered in the No. column. Column
headings 4J through 18 denote days 4 July though 18 July 1943. The number entry for a given
unit on a given day is the unit number (from the No. column) of the parent unit to which the
given unit is attached on that day. The dummy unit ID named UNATTACHED is listed as unit
No. 78. (No unit numbers 76 and 77 are listed.) Units in the table which have UNATTACHED
as a parent are actually not attached to any parent unit on that day. Each parent unit, except for
the dummy unit, UNATTACHED, is listed in the table as attached to itself on each day. Each
primary German combat unit listed in Table 3-1 is a parent unit in Table D-l, and there are no
other German parent units. Example attachment relationships derivable from Table D-l include:

    a. Illustrative Example 1. Unit No. 23 is entered in the 4J column of Table D-l only for
units No. 23, No. 41, and No.71, signifying that LSSAH (unit No. 23) is attached to itself on 4
July, and 861st Artillery Bn (unit No. 41) and 55th Nebelwerfer Rgt (unit No. 71) are the only
other units attached to it on that day.

    b. Illustrative Example 2. Unit No. 78 is entered in the 4J column of Table D-l only for
unit No. 66, signifying that 2/III/101st Art Rgt (unit No. 66) is the only combat unit not attached
to any parent unit on that day.

                                           APPENDIXE

                   UNIT COMBAT POSTURES AND CONTACT STATUS


E-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix shows tables with daily contact status and combat
posture status for the 48 Soviet primary line combat units and 17 German primary line combat
units in the KDB force. The data shown is an exact representation of status as recorded in the
KDB. No contact status or combat posture was recorded for headquarters units (those units of
type HQ in Tables 3-1 and 3-2). Keys to the meanings of the status codes shown in tables in this
appendix are:

    a. Contact Status Code Meanings (code symbols are enclosed in' ')

        (1) '+' indicates a unit actively engaged in combat. The unit is directly participating in
an attack or is being directly assaulted by an enemy.

        (2) '-' indicates an inactive unit which is within contact in the front line, but is not
participating in an attack, nor is being assaulted by an enemy.

        (3) ' ' A blank entry denotes a unit out of contact and not in the front line.

    b. Combat Posture Code Meanings (code symbols are enclosed in' ')

        (1) 'A' indicates attack posture, in which a unit is attempting to attack an enemy unit.

       (2) 'D' indicates delay posture in which a unit is deliberately withdrawing before the
enemy, but still attempting to make contact.

        (3) 'H' indicates a hasty defense posture in which a unit is defending from a position that
it has occupied for less than 3 days, or has not fortified.

       (4) *P' indicates a prepared defense posture in which a unit is defending in a position
prepared for defense, or has fallen back into a position prepared for defense.

       (5) 'O' indicates a posture that cannot be identified as one of the above postures.
Usually, this is any reserve position or transit movement.

The above meanings are the descriptions used in the KDB documentation.

E-2. DAILY UNIT CONTACT STATUS. Tables E-l and E-2 show the daily contact status of
German and Soviet line combat units, respectively. Column headings 4J through 18 denote days
4 July through 18 July 1943. The tabulated units consist of all of the units listed in Tables 3-1
and 3-2 which are not unit type HQ. Units are listed in the same order that they appear in Tables
3-1 and 3-2. The meanings of the tabulated entries are given in paragraph E-l.

                                           APPENDIX F

            DATA TABLES FOR PERSONNEL STATUS IN GERMAN UNITS


F-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing personnel statistics for
individual German units in the KDB. Statistics are shown only for the 24 primary combat units
listed in Table 3-1. As noted in Chapter 2, personnel in small units attached to these primary
units on a day are included in primary unit assets. There is no double counting. The units
attached to each primary unit on each day are shown in Appendix D. Units that are not attached
to any primary parent combat unit on a day have their assets combined into a dummy unit
named UNATTACHED, which is listed as a regular unit in the tables. Daily status is recorded in
the KDB as of 1800 on the indicated day. The personnel status categories for a specified day are:

    a. OH denotes onhand effective personnel present for duty.

    b. TOT CAS denotes total casualties.

   c. CBT CAS denotes combat casualties, which are defined as the total casualties after
excluding DNBI casualties. Combat casualties = KIA + CMIA + WIA.

    d. KIA denotes killed in action.

    e. CMIA denotes captured/missing in action.

    f. WIA denotes wounded in action.

    g. DNBI denotes disease/nonbattle casualties.

   h. REPLACED denotes replacement personnel received or transferred that day.

   i. RETURNS primarily denotes personnel returning from medical treatment above division.

F-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left corner of
each table. The units are listed in the same order used in Table 3-1. There is a column entry in
each row (personnel category) for each calendar day in July 1943 from 4 (July) through 18
(July). A blank entry indicates no information in that category recorded that day in the KDB for
that unit. Row (category) totals over the KDB scenario are given in the rightmost column for all
categories except onhand.

                                           APPENDIX G

              DATA TABLES FOR PERSONNEL STATUS IN SOVIET UNITS


 G-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing personnel statistics for
individual Soviet units in the KDB. Statistics are shown only for the 48 primary combat units
listed in Table 3-2. As noted in Chapter 2, personnel in small units attached to these primary
units on a day are included in primary unit assets. There is no double counting. The units
attached to each primary unit on each day are shown in Appendix D. Units that are not attached
to any parent on a day have their assets combined either into assets of a dummy unit named
UNATTACHED, if that unit is attached to a parent on at least 1 day of the campaign, or into
assets of a dummy unit named OTHER NONDIV, if that unit is never attached to a parent during
the campaign. Each of these dummy units is listed like a regular unit in the tables. Daily status
is recorded in the KDB as of 1800 on the indicated day. The personnel status categories are:

    a. OH denotes onhand effective personnel present for duty.

    b. TOT CAS denotes total casualties.

    c. CBT CAS denotes combat casualties, which are defined as the total casualties after
excluding DNBI casualties. Combat casualties = KIA + CMIA + WIA.

    d. KIA denotes killed in action.

    e. CMIA denotes captured/missing in action.

    f. WIA denotes wounded in action.

    g. DNBI denotes disease/nonbattle casualties.

    h. REPLACED denotes replacement personnel received or transferred that day. A negative
entry denotes replacements transferred out of the unit.

   i. RETURNS primarily denotes personnel returning from medical treatment above division.

G-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left corner of
each table. The units are listed in the same order used in Table 3-2. There is a column entry in
each row (personnel category) for each calendar day in July 1943 from 4 (July) through 18
(July). A blank entry indicates no information in that category recorded that day in the KDB for
that unit. Row (category) totals over the KDB scenario are given in the rightmost column for all
categories except onhand.

                                        APPENDIX H

              DATA TABLES FOR WEAPON STATUS IN GERMAN UNITS


H-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing weapon statistics for
individual German units in the KDB. Statistics reflect status as recorded in the KDB. Tables are
shown only for the 24 primary combat units listed in Table 3-1. As noted in Chapter 2, weapon
assets in small units attached to these primary units on a day are included in the primary unit
assets. There is no double counting. The units attached to each primary unit on each day are
shown in Appendix D. Units that are not attached to any primary parent combat unit on a day
have their assets combined into a dummy unit named UNATTACHED, which is listed as a
regular unit in the tables. Daily status in the KDB is as of 1800 on the indicated day. The
weapon status categories are:

   a. OH denotes onhand effective weapons.

   b. DST + ABND denotes total destroyed plus total abandoned weapons.

   c. DAMAGED denotes number of items damaged in action.

     d. ESf REPAIR denotes items in repair. According to KDB documentation, this field is
strictly optional and usually is not used in the KDB.

   e. REPLACED denotes number of items received as replacements.

   f. RETURNS primarily denotes number of items returning to operational status from repair.

H-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left corner of
each table. The order and nomenclature of units is the same as that used in Table 3-1. For each
weapon status category in each tabulated unit, there is a column entry in each row (weapon type)
for each calendar day from 4 (July) through 18 (July) in 1943. Row (weapon type) totals over
the KDB scenario are given in the rightmost column for all weapon status categories except
ONHAND. A weapon type is listed under a weapon status category only if at least 1 day has a
nonzero table entry in that status category. If the KDB records no weapons in a weapon status
category for a unit, the name ALL is listed in that category with all zero entries. The
classification and nomenclature of weapon types is essentially that used in the KDB. Many of
the abbreviations are defined in the glossary, but the user is referred to the KDB documentation
for details on vehicle/weapon model numbers and characteristics.

                                         APPENDIX I

               DATA TABLES FOR WEAPON STATUS IN SOVIET UNITS


1-1. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing weapon statistics for
individual Soviet units in the KDB. Statistics reflect status as recorded in the KDB. Tables are
shown only for the 67 primary combat units listed in Table 3-2. As noted in Chapter 2, weapon
assets in small units attached to these primary units on a day are included in the primary unit
assets. There is no double counting. The units attached to each primary unit on each day are
shown in Appendix D. Units that are not attached to any primary parent combat unit on a day
have their assets combined either into a dummy unit called UNATTACHED, if that unit is
attached to a parent on at least 1 day of the campaign, or into a dummy unit called OTHER
NONDIV if that unit is never attached to a parent during the campaign. Each of these dummy
units is listed as a regular unit in the tables. Daily status in the KDB is as of 1800 on the
indicated day. The weapon status categories are:

   a. OH denotes onhand effective weapons.

   b. DST + ABND denotes total destroyed plus total abandoned weapons.

   c. DAMAGED denotes number of items damaged in action.

     d. IN REPAIR denotes items in repair. According to KDB documentation, this field is
strictly optional and is usually not used in the KDB.

    e. REPLACED denotes number of items received or transferred as replacements. Negative
values denote items transferred out of a unit to serve as replacements elsewhere.

   f. RETURNS primarily denotes number of items returning to operational status from repair.

1-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left corner of
each table. The order and nomenclature of units is the same as that used in Table 3-2. For each
weapon status category in each tabulated unit, there is a column entry in each row (weapon type)
for each calendar day from 4 (July) through 18 (July) in 1943. Row (weapon type) totals over
the KDB scenario are given in the rightmost column for all weapon status categories except
ONHAND. A weapon type is listed under a weapon status category only if at least 1 day has a
nonzero table entry in that status category. If the KDB records no weapons in a weapon status
category for a unit, the name ALL is listed in that category with all zero entries. The
classification and nomenclature of weapon types is essentially that used in the KDB. Many of
the abbreviations are defined in the glossary, but the user is referred to the KDB documentation
for details on vehicle/weapon model numbers and characteristics.

                                         APPENDIX J

                       AMMUNITION STATUS IN GERMAN UNITS


J-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing ammunition statistics for
individual German units in the KDB. Statistics reflect status as recorded in the KDB. Tables are
shown only for the 24 primary combat units listed in Table 3-1. As noted in Chapter 2,
ammunition assets in small units attached to these primary units on a day are included in the
primary unit assets. There is no double counting. The units attached to each primary unit on
each day are shown in Appendix D. Daily status in the KDB is as of 1800 on the indicated day.
Tabulated tonnage is in short tons. Further descriptions of ammunition type status categories can
be found in the KDB documentation. The ammunition type status categories are:

   a. T/AT OH denoting onhand tank/antitank ammunition tonnage.

   b. ARTY OH denoting onhand artillery tonnage.

   c. RKT OH denoting onhand rocket tonnage.

    d. OTHER OH denoting onhand small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon
tonnage.

   e. T/AT USED denoting tank/antitank ammunition tonnage expended or consumed.

   f. ARTY USED denoting artillery tonnage expended or consumed.

    g. RKT USED denoting rocket tonnage expended or consumed.

   h. OTHER USED denoting small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon tonnage
expended or consumed.

    i. T/AT RECD denoting tank/antitank ammunition tonnage received.

   j. ARTY RECD denoting artillery tonnage received.

    k. RKT RECD denoting rocket tonnage received.

    1. OTHER RECD denoting small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon tonnage
received.

Negative numbers in OH and RECD categories indicate net tonnage due out of a unit. The data
do not always "balance," in an accounting sense. The change in daily onhand tonnage often
differs from (previous onhand + received - used). Several units use ammunition with zero
inventory tonnage onhand and received. Nevertheless, these data reflect the most complete
ammunition accounting available from the unit records.

CAA-SR-98-7



3-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left comer of
each table. The order and nomenclature of units is the same as that used in Table 3-1. For each
ammunition status category in each tabulated unit, there is a column entry in each row
(ammunition type/status) for each calendar day from 4 (July) through 18 (July) in 1943. Row
totals over the KDB timeframe are given in the rightmost column for all ammunition type status
categories except ONHAND. The classification of ammunition types is that used in the KDB.

                                         APPENDIX K

                        AMMUNITION STATUS IN SOVIET UNITS


K-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing ammunition statistics for
individual Soviet units in the KDB. Statistics reflect status as recorded in the KDB. Tables are
shown only for the 67 primary combat units listed in Table 3-2. As noted in Chapter 2,
ammunition assets in small units attached to these primary units on a day are included in the
primary unit assets. There is no double counting. The units attached to each primary unit on
each day are shown in Appendix D. Daily status in the KDB is as of 1800 on the indicated day.
Tabulated tonnage is in short tons. Further descriptions of ammunition type status categories can
be found in the KDB documentation. The ammunition type status categories are:

    a. T/AT OH denoting onhand tank/antitank ammunition tonnage.

    b. ARTY OH denoting onhand artillery tonnage.

    c. RKT OH denoting onhand rocket tonnage.

    d. OTHER OH denoting onhand small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon
tonnage.

    e. T/AT USED denoting tank/antitank ammunition tonnage expended or consumed.

    f. ARTY USED denoting artillery tonnage expended or consumed.

    g. RKT USED denoting rocket tonnage expended or consumed.

   h. OTHER USED denoting small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon tonnage
expended or consumed.

   i. T/AT RECD denoting tank/antitank ammunition tonnage received.

   j. ARTY RECD denoting artillery tonnage received.

   k. RKT RECD denoting rocket tonnage received.

    I. OTHER RECD denoting small arms, antiaircraft, and miscellaneous weapon tonnage
received.

Negative numbers in OH and RECD categories indicate net tonnage due out of a unit.




                                                                                         K-l
CAA-SR-98-7


K-2. FORMAT OF DATA TABLES. The unit ID (name) is given in the upper left comer of
each table. The order and nomenclature of units is the same as that used in Table 3-2. For each
ammunition status category in each tabulated unit, there is a column entry in each row
(ammunition type/status) for each calendar day from 4 (July) through 18 (July) in 1943. Row
totals over the KDB timeframe are given in the rightmost column for all ammunition type status
categories except ONHAND. The classification of ammunition types is that used in the KDB.

                                          APPENDIX L

                 DAILY LOCATIONS OF GERMAN AND SOVIET UNITS


L-l. INTRODUCTION. This appendix contains data tables showing daily unit locations for
individual German and Soviet units in the KDB. As noted in Chapter 2 and Chapter 8, each
unit's location on a day was computed as the arithmetic average of the locations of the KDB
reference points and flank location points, excluding the HQ location point, which are listed in
the KDB for that unit on that day. Using a fitting equation, these locations were converted from
UTM locations into locations expressed in terms of latitude and longitude. The HQ location was
not used in the calculation of unit location, unless it was the only point listed, because the HQ
often is positioned noticeably behind (to the rear of) the body of other points comprising the unit
in the KDB. There is no clear "best way" to define and compute a KDB unit location. The
author selected the one used herein as suitable for the statistics derived from it. Readers may
define and compute their own unit locations using the latitude-longitude location data for all
KDB reference points which are contained in the CD ROM on the Battle of Kursk (Ref 4).

L-2. STRUCTURE OF DATA TABLES. Tables L-l and L-2 show daily unit locations for
German and Soviet units, respectively. A daily location is only shown for a unit for if at least
one reference point is recorded in the KDB on that day. The units in the tables are from the units
in Tables 3-1 and 3-2 of Chapter 3. Each line in Tables L-l and L-2 shows the following data:

    a. Date is a Julian date (e.g. 19430704 denotes 4 July 1943).

    b. Unit Name is taken from the Unit JD column of Tables 3-1 and 3-2.

     c. In the Deg Lat column, N denotes north latitude, and the number immediately following it
is the degrees of (north) latitude for the unit location, as defined above. In the Deg Long
column, E denotes east longitude. Immediately following it is the associated degrees (east)
longitude for the unit location. No minutes and seconds are computed; instead, degrees are
expressed to three decimal places.

    d. The Nr Pts column gives the total number of KDB reference points recorded for that unit
on that day in the KDB.

Any unrecognized errors in data entry for individual points during construction of the KDB will
have been carried over into unit location computations listed here.

2. DEFINITIONS

combat casualties
   combat casualties = KIA + CMIA + WIA

daily average combat casualty rate
    The daily average combat casualty rate of a force is the arithmetic average of the daily unit
casualty rates over all line units engaged in combat on that day. A line unit is defined as engaged
in combat on a day if it sustains more than one combat casualty on that day.

daily unit combat casualty rate
    A unit's daily combat casualty rate is the number of combat casualties incurred per 1,000
onhand (at start of day) men in that unit on that day.

force ratio
    For a Red military force opposing a Blue force, the force ratio favoring side Red is defined
as: [total onhand Red items] / [total onhand Blue items] where the items are personnel or
weapon systems in the force.

fractional exchange ratio
   For a Red military force opposing a Blue force, the fractional exchange ratio favoring side
Blue in a time period I is defined as

(ALOSSESRED(i)/ALOSSESBLUE(i))/[Force Ratio „]

where ALOSSESRED(i) = total losses of specified Red items in period i,
     ALOSSESBLUE(i) = total losses of specified Blue items during period i,
and Force Ratio (l) = force ratio favoring Red at start of period i.
